title: Phoning Dexter and her home recordings
summary: After hesitating she called Dexter, met him, mentioned her home records made on a Packard Bell, and learned her brother Joe had played him some without telling her.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Capitol Records wanted to hear from me, wanted me to get in touch with him. Well, I didn't do it right away. I hesitated. It was two or three days. Because I had been disappointed. And I said, well, two or three days after that, I said well, I'll give Mr. Dexter a call. So when I called, well his little secretary, who was Marilyn Hammond --
I don't know if you remember her.

Marilyn Hammond who was just a darling, she was just a darling girl. And so Marilyn said, 'Oh, yes, Mr. Dexter's waiting to hear from you, Miss Lutcher.' I said, 'Well, would you give him my number and tell him to call.' And she said, 'Well, he will call you as soon as he gets in.' So sure enough, he did call me and he and I chatted and he told me he wanted me to come up, you know. He said, 'Well, I'd love for you to come up to the office here. I'd like to talk with you.' And so in the next two or three days, well, it ended up that way. I went up and had a chat with him, and it all -- you know, he asked me had I ever recorded before, which I had not. I had never recorded for any label or anything. I had made some home records, because I used to have a little Packard Bell, which was -- Packard Bell at that time used to put out a tremendous recorder. It was absolutely terrific.

Yeah. I think I have some of those old home records now, and I just made them at home, you know, just to hear how my material, stuff, would sound. You know. And I said, "No, I've never recorded for anyone." And he said he had heard something of mine. My brother Joe had taken some little things, little home records or something, you know, up there for him to hear, and he didn't particularly care for what he heard, you know, on the record, but he said, "I like you. Your brother brought some things up here and I told your brother to have you contact me," but my brother didn't tell me. I don't know if he forgot, I just don't know, but all I know is I didn't get the message, you know. And I says, "Well, I didn't know that you had told him to tell me." And he says, "Yes, I told your brother to have you get in touch with me." And he said, "I want you to make some -- I just want you to make some tests." At that time you could go to some of the studios. There were a lot of studios around, and he said, "I want you to go to the studio, Nellie, and make a few things. I just want to get an idea of what your voice sounds like on records," you know. Because everybody who maybe has a style and can sing or has a voice, you know, they don't record well. There are a lot of people who don't record well. Like Arthur Lee Simpkins was one of the finest vocalists ever, but he never really recorded. He never.
